content: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in infants under six months of age is a significant global public health issue, contributing to over one million deaths of young children annually. While most research and treatment efforts have historically focused on children aged six to 59 months, there is growing evidence that SAM is also a critical problem among infants younger than six months. This age group has often been overlooked in both research and operational programs, despite its importance. The World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned this review to address the evidence gap regarding the inpatient treatment of SAM in infants under six months. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Background SAM in infants under six months is often underestimated due to the misconception that exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) protects this age group from malnutrition. However, global rates of EBF are strikingly low, with only 25–31% of infants aged two to five months being exclusively breastfed. Additionally, the adoption of WHO Child Growth Standards (WHO-GS) has led to a higher prevalence of SAM being identified in this age group compared to older growth references, such as those from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Treatment of SAM in infants under six months is particularly challenging. These infants are not traditionally considered eligible for ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTFs) due to recommendations for EBF during the first six months of life. Instead, treatment focuses on re-establishing EBF, which is time-intensive and requires skilled staff—resources that are often scarce in settings where SAM is most prevalent. Consequently, there is limited capacity to address SAM in this age group, and proactive case finding is rare, unlike the active detection strategies used for older children. Methods The review involved two main components: 1. Appraisal of National Guidelines: The authors reviewed 36 national SAM treatment guidelines to determine current recommendations for managing SAM in infants under six months. The AGREE (Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation) framework was used to assess the quality and content of these guidelines. 2. GRADE Review of Published Literature: The authors conducted a systematic review of the literature to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of therapeutic feeding strategies for inpatient treatment of SAM in infants under six months. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework was applied to assess the quality of evidence. Key Findings 1. National Guidelines: Of the 36 guidelines reviewed, 29 (81%) included specific sections on SAM in infants under six months. However, the space devoted to this age group was limited, averaging only 6% of the total guideline content. All 29 guidelines recommended inpatient treatment for SAM in this age group. Only one guideline distinguished between clinically complicated and uncomplicated cases, as is done for older children. Supplementary suckling (SS) was recommended as the core treatment strategy in 28 of the 29 guidelines, with the aim of re-establishing effective EBF. Strengths of the guidelines included clear articulation of scope and purpose, good stakeholder involvement, clarity of presentation, and tools to support applicability. However, major weaknesses included a lack of patient involvement, poor rigor in development, and insufficient editorial independence. 2. GRADE Review: High-quality evidence for key questions regarding therapeutic feeding strategies was lacking. This represents both a weakness (current guidelines are based on low-quality evidence) and an opportunity (there is significant scope for research and improvement). The review highlighted the need for better evidence on the safest and most effective therapeutic feeding strategies during the stabilization, transition, and rehabilitation phases of treatment. Questions remain about the optimal type of milk, feeding volumes, feeding protocols, and modes of feeding (e.g., supplementary suckling, cup feeding, or spoon feeding). Recommendations 1. Infants with SAM should be divided into two groups: those with the potential to breastfeed and those without. This distinction is critical for tailoring treatment strategies. 2. Low-birth-weight (LBW) infants should follow the WHO 2010 LBW guidelines, which may also apply to SAM infants of unknown birth weight. 3. Age should be considered during assessment and treatment decisions. 4. For stabilization feeds, infant formula at 100 kcal/kg/day is a strong option due to its similarity to breast milk, low renal solute load, and availability of lactose-free varieties. However, this recommendation is conditional on the availability of appropriate feeds. 5. For transition and rehabilitation feeds, breast milk substitutes (BMS) such as formula or F-100 should be stepped up for non-breastfed infants, while breastfed infants should transition to exclusive breastfeeding as breast milk is re-established. Discussion The lack of high-quality evidence has not prevented progress in addressing SAM in infants under six months at the country level. However, current approaches are markedly different from those for older children, with no separation of complicated and uncomplicated cases and no outpatient-based or public health-focused models of care. Future research is urgently needed to address these gaps and improve international guidance. The current lack of gold-standard evidence presents an opportunity for research and innovation. Even acknowledging the issue of SAM in infants under six months would be a significant step forward and could stimulate further work in this area. Specific guidance arising from this review includes optimizing nutrition and fluid intake, supporting breastfeeding caregivers, addressing psychosocial issues, and linking nutrition programs with other healthcare initiatives. Conclusion With increasing recognition of the long-term and short-term impacts of early-life nutrition, there has never been a better time to tackle SAM in infants under six months. This review contributes to that goal by synthesizing current evidence and identifying key areas for future research and guideline development.
